message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"3.11","text":"Therefore, before everything else, one ought to know that one finds it nowhere except from a prophet of truth. A true prophet is one who always knows everything, including the thoughts of everyone, and is sinless, as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment. Therefore, we ought not to consider his foreknowledge superficially, but to ask whether his foreknowledge can subsist without any other basis. For physicians foretell things while having the sick person’s pulse as material laid before them; some do so by means of birds, others by means of sacrificial victims, and still others foretell while having many other different materials laid before them—and they are not prophets.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"αὐτὴν","chosen":"it","rationale":"The feminine pronoun’s antecedent lies outside the supplied passage; “it” preserves the unresolved reference, probably to truth."},{"source_quote":"προφήτου ἀληθείας","chosen":"a prophet of truth","rationale":"Retains the source’s genitive expression rather than replacing it with the interpretive “true prophet,” which appears explicitly in the next sentence."},{"source_quote":"ὡς περὶ θεοῦ κρίσεως πεπληροφορημένος","chosen":"as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment","rationale":"πεπληροφορημένος denotes being fully convinced or assured; “fully informed” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ἄνευ ἑτέρας προφάσεως","chosen":"without any other basis","rationale":"In context πρόφασις denotes an external ground, occasion, or means on which a prediction depends, not merely a verbal pretext."},{"source_quote":"ὑποβεβλημένην ὕλην","chosen":"material laid before them","rationale":"The phrase presents the pulse and divinatory objects as supplied data or material underlying the predictions."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.12","text":"But if someone should wish to say that foreknowledge by way of such predictions is similar to genuinely innate foreknowledge, that person is greatly deceived. For things of this kind disclose only what is present, and that only if they prove true. Yet in another respect even these are useful to me, for they establish that foreknowledge exists. But the foreknowledge of the one true prophet not only knows what is present but extends its prophecy without limit as far as the coming age itself, and it needs nothing for understanding; and, of prophecies, dim and ambiguous things, so that what is said should need another prophet for understanding, but explicit and plain things, just as our teacher, being also a prophet, always knew everything by an innate and ever-flowing spirit.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὴν διὰ τῶν τοιούτων προρρήσεων","chosen":"foreknowledge by way of such predictions","rationale":"The article points to an implied feminine noun, most naturally πρόγνωσις from the immediate context."},{"source_quote":"ἄλλως δέ μοι καὶ αὐτὰ εὐχρηστεῖ","chosen":"Yet in another respect even these are useful to me","rationale":"ἄλλως marks a different respect in which the practices support the author’s argument, despite not constituting true prophecy."},{"source_quote":"ἡ δὲ τοῦ μόνου καὶ ἀληθοῦς πρόγνωσις","chosen":"the foreknowledge of the one true prophet","rationale":"“Prophet” is contextually supplied after the substantival “the one and true”; the more formally literal alternative is “the foreknowledge of the only and true one.”"},{"source_quote":"μέχρις αὐτοῦ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος ἀπέραντον ἐκτείνει τὴν προφητείαν","chosen":"extends its prophecy without limit as far as the coming age itself","rationale":"ἀπέραντον characterizes the prophecy as unlimited, while μέχρις marks its stated reach to the coming age."},{"source_quote":"ἐνφύτῳ καὶ ἀεννάῳ πνεύματι","chosen":"by an innate and ever-flowing spirit","rationale":"ἀένναος evokes something perpetually flowing or unfailing; “perennial” or “unceasing” are viable alternatives."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"καὶ οὐδενὸς δεῖται πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, καὶ προφητειῶν ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, ἵνα ἄλλου προφήτου χρείαν ἔχῃ τὰ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, ἀλλὰ ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ","issue":"The selected reading does not yield defensible continuous syntax. The genitive προφητειῶν is followed by accusative neuter adjectives ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, and the contrast with ἀλλὰ ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ lacks a supported predicate or negation. The English reflects the resulting fracture rather than silently supplying the apparent intended claim.","proposed_reading":"One possible conjecture is καὶ οὐ προφητεύει ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, ἵνα ἄλλου προφήτου χρείαν ἔχῃ τὰ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, ἀλλὰ ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ (“and it does not prophesy dim and ambiguous things, so that what is said needs another prophet for understanding, but explicit and plain things”). This is conjectural and is not substituted into the translation.","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"3.13","text":"Therefore, he confidently gave an account of what was going to happen—I mean sufferings, places, and limits. For, being an unerring prophet, surveying everything with the boundless eye of the soul, he knows it all while himself escaping notice. But if we too admit, as most people do, that even the true prophet has foreknowledge not always but only at times—when he has the spirit and, for that reason, foreknows, but when he does not have it, is ignorant—if we suppose this, we will both deceive ourselves and lay snares for others. For such a thing belongs to those madly inspired by a spirit of disorder, those becoming drunk beside altars and being filled with the reek of burnt fat.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πάθη, τόπους, ὅρους","chosen":"sufferings, places, and limits","rationale":"ὅροι can denote boundaries, limits, or termini; “limits” preserves the term without conflating it with the explicitly named times in 3.15."},{"source_quote":"ἀπείρῳ ψυχῆς ὀφθαλμῷ","chosen":"with the boundless eye of the soul","rationale":"Preserves both the singular eye image and ἄπειρος in its sense of boundless or unlimited."},{"source_quote":"ἐπίσταται λανθάνων","chosen":"he knows it all while himself escaping notice","rationale":"λανθάνων most naturally describes the prophet as remaining unnoticed while knowing; “he knows secretly” is a possible but less formally precise alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἄλλους ἐνεδρεύσομεν","chosen":"lay snares for others","rationale":"ἐνεδρεύω denotes lying in wait for or entrapping someone, not merely making an intellectual mistake."},{"source_quote":"κνίσης ἐνφορουμένων","chosen":"being filled with the reek of burnt fat","rationale":"κνίσα is the smoke, steam, or odor of sacrificial fat; “sacrificial fumes” is a viable less vivid alternative."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.14","text":"For if someone wishing to profess prophecy is allowed to be believed, in the matters in which he is caught as a liar, that at that time he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge, he will not be easy to expose, though he is a prophet who is a liar. For in the cases where, while saying many things, he hits upon a few, he is then believed to have the spirit. Moreover, he speaks of first things as last and last things as first, things that have happened as things that will happen, and things that will happen as though they had already happened. He also says other, incoherent things, things stolen from others and transformed, and some things curtailed, shapeless, senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear, all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα","chosen":"he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge","rationale":"Preserves the source’s attributive relation between the holy spirit and foreknowledge without identifying it with a later doctrinal formulation."},{"source_quote":"ὡς πολλὰ λέγων ὀλίγα ἐπιτυγχάνει","chosen":"while saying many things, he hits upon a few","rationale":"ἐπιτυγχάνει describes occasionally hitting the mark or obtaining a correct result among numerous claims."},{"source_quote":"ἐξ ἄλλων ὑφῃρημένα","chosen":"things stolen from others","rationale":"ὑφαιρέω can mean taking away secretly; “appropriated from others” is a less pointed alternative."},{"source_quote":"μεμειωμένα","chosen":"curtailed","rationale":"The perfect passive describes things reduced, diminished, or mutilated; “curtailed” fits the treatment of allegedly defective predictions."},{"source_quote":"ἀνείδεα","chosen":"shapeless","rationale":"The spelling supports ἀνειδής, “without form, shapeless, unsightly,” rather than ἀναιδής, “shameless.”"},{"source_quote":"πάσης κεκραγότα δυσσυνειδησίας","chosen":"all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience","rationale":"κεκραγότα is vivid language for openly betraying or proclaiming something; δυσσυνειδησία can denote a bad or guilty conscience and, by extension, unscrupulousness."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.15","text":"But our teacher resorted to no such trickery. Rather, as I said earlier, being a prophet who always knew everything by an innate and ever-flowing spirit, he confidently set things out, clearly foretelling sufferings, places, fixed times, ways, and limits. For example, when foretelling about the sanctuary, he said, “Do you see these buildings? Amen, I tell you, not one stone upon another will be left here that will not be torn down,” and, “This generation will certainly not pass away, and the demolition will have its beginning. For they will come and encamp here and throw up an encircling stockade and slaughter your children here.” Likewise, he spoke what follows in a clear voice, things that we are able to see with our own eyes, so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur. For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"οὐδέν τι τοιοῦτο ἐγοητεύσατο","chosen":"resorted to no such trickery","rationale":"γοητεύω can denote practicing sorcery, bewitching, or deceiving as a charlatan; “trickery” preserves the polemical accusation without asserting literal magic."},{"source_quote":"ἐμφύτῳ καὶ ἀεννάῳ πνεύματι","chosen":"by an innate and ever-flowing spirit","rationale":"The same wording as in 3.12 is rendered consistently; “unceasing spirit” is also possible for ἀένναος."},{"source_quote":"ἐνπροθέσμους χρόνους","chosen":"fixed times","rationale":"The adjective describes times set or bounded in advance; “appointed times” is a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"περὶ τοῦ ἁγιάσματος","chosen":"about the sanctuary","rationale":"ἁγίασμα denotes a holy place or sanctuary; “temple” would be a contextual identification rather than the source’s exact designation."},{"source_quote":"ἀμὴν ὑμῖν λέγω","chosen":"Amen, I tell you","rationale":"Retains the distinctive introductory formula rather than replacing it with the familiar interpretive rendering “Truly, I tell you.”"},{"source_quote":"καθιοῦσιν ἐνταῦθα","chosen":"encamp here","rationale":"The future form conveys sitting or settling down; in the military context, “encamp” is natural, while “sit down here” is the more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"περιχαρακώσουσιν","chosen":"throw up an encircling stockade","rationale":"The verb denotes enclosing with a palisade or stockade. The Greek supplies no explicit object, so the English likewise avoids specifying whom or what is enclosed."},{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς","chosen":"Likewise","rationale":"The adverb can mean “equally” or “all the same”; “nevertheless” is possible, but continuation by similarity best fits the immediate context."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς γὰρ πίστιν ἀκουόντων τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀποδείξεως ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας ποιεῖται προφήτης","chosen":"For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear","rationale":"λόγον ποιεῖσθαι can mean formulating or delivering an account, while πρὸς πίστιν gives its intended effect. “Gives an account of the demonstration for the faith of the hearers” is a more formal alternative."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
